latin: Victor, sex annos natus<sup>1</sup>, optat ut pater sibi tympanum emat.
Pater autem: «Nolo, nam me laborantem impedires<sup>2</sup>».
Nequaquam, respondet Victor, tibi enim polliceor<sup>3</sup> me tantum te dormiente tympanum pulsaturum esse<sup>4</sup>.
Mater. — Nolo, Jacobe<sup>5</sup>, ludas cum Leone, nam puerulus est male educatus.
Jacobus. — Tunc, Mater, visne Leonem mecum ludere<sup>6</sup>, nam ego puerulus<sup>7</sup> sum bene educatus?
Cum bellum<sup>8</sup> omnium gentium alterum ageretur, cibariorum<sup>9</sup> tanta facta est inopia...
ut<sup>10</sup> vir quidam, fame<sup>11</sup> laborans, canem suum, quem multum amabat, edere coactus sit<sup>12</sup>.
Postquam manducavit, ossa aspiciens, secum exclamavit:
Miselle<sup>13</sup> Mordax, quam bene cenares, si hic adesses<sup>14</sup>.
Canes qui vehementius latrant, habentur viliores.
english: Victor, [aged] six (born six years), [would like] (wishes) his father to buy him a drum.
But [his] father [replies]: “[No] (I don't want), for you would [stop me working] (me working you would hinder).”
Not at all, replies Victor, [I promise you] that I will only play the drum [when you are asleep] (to you I promise me only you sleeping drum to be about to beat).
The mother. — James, I don't want you to play with Leo, for he's a badly brought-up little child.
James. — Then, mummy, do you want Leo to play with me, because I'm a well-brought-up little child?
During the Second [World] War (of all nations... was being waged), there was such a shortage of [food] (things relating to nourishment)...
that a man, who was suffering from hunger, was obliged to eat his dog, which he loved very much.
After he had eaten, looking at the bones, he exclaimed [to himself]:
Poor Mordax, how well you would dine, if you were here.
The dogs that bark (the) loudest are [considered] (held for) the most contemptible (= the smaller they are, the more they bark).

footnotes: Natus, perfect participle of nascor, -eris, -i, natus sum, to be born.

Te dormiente, you sleeping: ABLATIVE ABSOLUTE embedded in the infinitive clause: polliceor me... pulsaturum esse. These last two words form a FUTURE INFINITIVE: future participle in -urus, -a, -um + present infinitive of the verb to be. Note that me is in the accusative and te in the ablative.
Jacobus, James or Jacob; Leo, Leonis, Leo; leo, as a common noun, the lion (f. leaena, -ae).
Visne: velle, irregular verb, here in the 2nd pers. sg. of the pres. ind., is construed with the infinitive clause.
Puerulus, diminutive of puer; f. puellula, from puella.
Cibarius, -a, -um, relating to nourishment (cibus, -i, m.); here neuter plural (used as a noun).

Tantus... ut: tantus, -a, -um, so great, goes in pairs, — either with quantus, -a, -um, how great (e.g. tantus quantum vis, there is [as much] (so great) work [as] (how great) you want); — or with ut (and then the subjunctive), as here.
Cogere = cum + agere, to force (cf. L. 46, N. 14); same conjugation as agere.
Cenares, adesses: imperfect subjunctives of cenare and adesse.
comments: Mors, mortis, f., death. — Velociter, atrociter, are adverbs formed from the adjectives atrox, atrocis and velox, velocis. — Nemo, neminis = ne homo, not a man, no person (ne). — Nihil = ne hilum, not a hilum (black dot on a seed), that is to say nothing. — Parcetur: future of parco, -is, -ere, peperci, parsum (note nemini in the dative), word for word: it will not be spared to anyone, no one will be spared. The 3rd person of the PASSIVE is sometimes used in place of our «one». Libet, it pleases; quodlibet, adj. demonstrative (n.), what one pleases: in other words, no matter which; cf. French un quolibet; the corresponding pronoun is quidlibet, no matter what; the forms quilibet (m.) and quaelibet (f.) are common to the pronoun and the adjective. — Flos, floris, is of masculine gender, like fiore in Italian.

latin: Vita nostra brevis est, brevi finietur. (bis)
english: Our life is short, it will soon end.
Long live the Academy! Long live the professors!
— Long live each member (of the Academy)!
— Long live all the members (of the Academy)!
— May they always be flourishing (in flower)!

sources.latin: E Vita Latina, A. Rodot, sept. 1961.
